title: Benjamini–Hochberg as a named FDR recipe
dek: Sort p, reject through the last k with p_(k)≤(k/m)α. Wikipedia algorithm. q-values and π0 stay on stats-fdr.
story: The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure on Wikipedia is an algorithm: sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k) ≤ (k/m) α, reject those k. Under independence (and some PRDS dependence) this controls FDR at α.
stats-fdr already explains q-values and Storey π0. This card is the named 1995 recipe so 'we used FDR' can be made precise.
BH is conservative when π0 ≪ 1. That is a feature of the bound, not a bug in your RNA-seq.
deep: The BH threshold is data-dependent: more small p-values licence a looser cut. That shocks Bonferroni users.
Positive dependence (PRDS) is the usual defence; one isolate driving every gene is not that defence.
BY (Benjamini–Yekutieli) pays extra for arbitrary dependence.
Do not call BH a FWER method.

visual.caption: BH as a procedure, not a posterior. q-values are a reporting layer on stats-fdr.

example.title: m=5, p=0.01, 0.04, 0.03, 0.20, 0.50, α=0.05

steps.title: 0.01≤0.01, 0.03>0.02, 0.04>0.03… wait 0.03 vs 0.02 fails. Largest k with inequality: k=1 only? Recheck: p(2)=0.03 vs 0.02 — no. So k̂=1.
If the second p had been 0.018, k would grow

example.takeaway: BH is a sorted-p algorithm. It is not Bonferroni with better branding.

check.why: Largest k satisfying the inequality is 3.

formulas.label: BH rule
formulas.note: Reject p_{(1)}…p_{(k̂)}; 0 if no such k.
